turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ugh, sorry we're late. Parking was a nightmare and the lady up front had to redo the whole insurance card.
[SEG0002] person_2 (NURSE): You're fine, we've been behind all morning. I'll grab a pressure real quick. My sister was like forty minutes late to her physical last week, the 405 was just stopped.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm. Hurry up, that cuff always hurts.
[SEG0004] person_2 (NURSE): Ok. One fifty eight over ninety two, heart rate 76. Med list shows amlodopine five milligrams and hydrochlorothyazide twenty five milligrams daily.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That water pill is wrong. Bottle I picked up says twelve and a half milligrams, not twenty five. You're on the old dose.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't care about the bottle right now. Can the doctor just come in. I've been on my feet forever.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hey. Sorry, this thing froze again. Uh, what brings you in? I missed whatever you just said.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): My ankles are all puffy and I'm peeing like every hour. That's why I came.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Puffy, ok. Say the peeing part again? A refill box popped up.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Every hour. Sometimes twice an hour. Worse at night. I'm wiped out and I'm sick of repeating myself.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Swelling and the bathroom, about three weeks. She just gets snappy, won't put her feet up.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Umm, you're still on the amlodopine, five milligrams every morning?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, by mouth, every morning. And the water pill, whatever it is. I stopped the lisinipril back in March, the cough was awful.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stopped lisinopril. Did they ever give you the potassium with that water pill, did you take it?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Never picked it up. I never took it. Can we move.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain? Or short of breath walking around?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. Not short of breath. It's the ankles and the peeing, I said that.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): How about your stomach, bowels, nausea, any of that?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Stomach's fine. No.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's had high blood pressure for years, that's the pills. Retired from the post office. Mostly on the couch now, which doesn't help anybody's mood.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hold on, wrong tab. Nurse has you at one fifty eight over ninety two. What was the home one, say it again?
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): This morning, 132 over 84. I wrote it on a receipt. Your machine runs high.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll use today's number. Let me see the ankles. Yeah, pitting edema both sides, the socks left a dent. Lungs are clear.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Don't tell me the heart's quitting. I do not have the energy today.

[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): I don't think it's your heart. The amlodipine opens the little vessels and fluid leaks out into the ankles, that's the puffiness. The water pill makes the kidneys dump salt and water, so you're in the bathroom constantly. It's the meds doing it.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Then change something. Please. I'm tired of this.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Err, I'm stopping the amlodipine. Switch to losartan, fifty milligrams, once a day by mouth, for the pressure. Start tomorrow.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Fifty, once a day. Fine. And the water pill, since you all can't agree?

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leave that dose alone till I see the bottle. Bring the actual bottle to the desk on your way out. I'm ordering a basic metabolic panel downstairs today, kidneys and the salts.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the bottle out front. She missed breakfast too, that's half the mood.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in four weeks. If you get real chest pain or you can't catch your breath, go to the ER, don't wait. Otherwise four weeks.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Ok. Let's go, I'm done.

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
